topics.title: File Uploads with Multer, Safety and Cloud Storage
topics.summary: Accept multipart uploads with multer, enforce size/type limits, and move files to Cloudinary or S3 instead of the server disk.
topics.description:
`express.json()` cannot read files. Uploads use `multipart/form-data`, parsed by **multer**, which adds `req.file` (single) or `req.files` (many) and puts text fields in `req.body`.

### Storage engines
- **diskStorage**: writes to a folder; you control destination and filename.
- **memoryStorage**: keeps a `Buffer` in `req.file.buffer`; good when forwarding straight to cloud storage (keep files small).

### Upload helpers
`upload.single('avatar')`, `upload.array('photos', 5)`, `upload.fields([{ name: 'cover' }, { name: 'docs' }])`. The string must match the form field name.

### File upload safety (important)
1. Set `limits: { fileSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024, files: 5 }`.
2. Use `fileFilter` to allow only expected MIME types - but the MIME type comes from the client, so also check the real **magic bytes** (package `file-type`) before trusting an image.
3. **Never** use the original filename for the path: generate a random name (`crypto.randomUUID()`) and keep only a safe extension. Original names can contain `../` or overwrite files.
4. Store uploads **outside** the web root or on object storage; never execute them.
5. Require authentication and rate-limit upload routes.
6. Scan or re-encode images (e.g. with `sharp`) for sensitive apps.

### Cloud storage
Local disks vanish on many hosts (Render, Heroku, containers). Use **Cloudinary** (upload stream, returns a CDN URL and handles image transformations) or **AWS S3 / R2** (store object keys; send the browser a pre-signed URL so large files go straight to storage, bypassing your server).

Save only the resulting URL or key in the database.
keyPoints: multer parses multipart; field name must match `single('name')`
Always set size/count limits and a `fileFilter`
Do not trust the client MIME type or filename; generate your own names
Use memory storage + cloud upload for ephemeral hosts
Store URLs/keys in the DB, not file bytes
pitfalls: Using `file.originalname` as the saved path (path traversal, overwrites)
No size limit (disk exhaustion) or no auth on the upload route
Relying on local disk in containers or serverless where it is wiped
Placing `upload.single()` after the body is already consumed by another parser

examples.title: Safe image upload with multer
Memory upload to Cloudinary (overview)
Test upload

interview.q: Why not trust file.mimetype or originalname?
interview.a: Both come from the client and can be forged; check magic bytes server-side and generate your own safe filename to prevent disguised files and path traversal.

interview.q: Why use Cloudinary or S3 instead of the server disk?
interview.a: Container and PaaS disks are ephemeral and not shared between instances; object storage is durable, scalable and can serve files via CDN.

topics.title: Real-time: Server-Sent Events and Socket.IO
topics.summary: Push data to browsers with one-way SSE or two-way Socket.IO and attach both to an Express server.
topics.description:
HTTP is request/response, so the server cannot push data by itself. Two common solutions:

### Server-Sent Events (SSE)
A long-lived HTTP response with `Content-Type: text/event-stream`. The server sends text messages; the browser's built-in `EventSource` receives them and **auto-reconnects**. It is **one-way** (server to client) and works over plain HTTP, ideal for notifications, progress bars, live dashboards and AI token streaming.

Message format: `data: <text>\n\n` (a blank line ends one event). Optional `event:` and `id:` fields. Remove the client from your list on `req.on('close')`, and send a periodic comment (`: ping`) to keep proxies from closing the connection. Disable proxy buffering in nginx (`proxy_buffering off`).

### Socket.IO (WebSockets)
A library for **two-way**, low-latency communication with rooms, namespaces, acknowledgements and automatic fallback/reconnection. Use it for chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing.

Setup: wrap the Express app in an `http.Server`, then attach `new Server(httpServer, { cors })`. On `connection` you get a `socket` to `emit` and listen with `on`. `io.to(room).emit()` broadcasts to a room. Authenticate in `io.use((socket, next) => ...)` using a token in `socket.handshake.auth`.

### Which one?
| Need | Choose |
|---|---|
| Server pushes updates only | SSE |
| Client and server both send often | Socket.IO / WebSocket |
| Simple, works with HTTP infra | SSE |
| Rooms, broadcast, presence | Socket.IO |

### Scaling
Several server instances need a shared adapter (Redis adapter for Socket.IO) so broadcasts reach every client.
keyPoints: SSE: `text/event-stream`, one-way, `EventSource` auto-reconnects
Clean up SSE clients on `req.on('close')`
Socket.IO needs `http.createServer(app)` and `new Server(httpServer)`
Authenticate sockets in `io.use` and use rooms for targeting
Scale Socket.IO with the Redis adapter and sticky sessions
pitfalls: Not configuring CORS for Socket.IO separately from Express
Leaking SSE connections (never removing closed clients)

examples.title: Server-Sent Events
Browser side
Socket.IO chat server

interview.a: SSE is one-way server-to-client over normal HTTP with built-in reconnection; WebSocket (and Socket.IO) is full duplex, better when the client also sends frequent messages.

interview.q: Why can't you just call app.listen when using Socket.IO?
interview.a: Socket.IO must attach to the underlying HTTP server; create it with http.createServer(app), pass it to Server, and call httpServer.listen.

topics.title: Sending Email with Nodemailer
topics.summary: Send transactional emails (welcome, verify, reset) via SMTP with nodemailer, ideally from a queue.
topics.description:
**Nodemailer** is the standard Node library for sending email over SMTP. In production you connect it to a provider (Gmail app password for demos, SendGrid, Mailgun, Amazon SES, Resend, Brevo) rather than running your own mail server.

### Steps
1. Create a **transporter** once with host, port, and credentials from `.env`.
2. Call `transporter.sendMail({ from, to, subject, text, html })`.
3. Handle failures: email delivery should not make the main request fail unexpectedly.

### Good practices
- Always provide both `text` and `html` versions.
- Use a verified sender domain with SPF/DKIM/DMARC DNS records, otherwise mail lands in spam.
- Escape user-provided values inserted in HTML.
- **Do not make users wait** for SMTP: respond first and send in the background, or push a job to a queue (BullMQ + Redis) with retries.
- Use `jsonTransport` or a fake SMTP (Ethereal, Mailpit, MailHog) in development and tests so no real emails go out.
- Never log full email bodies containing tokens.

### Templates
Generate HTML from template strings, Handlebars/EJS, or the `mjml` library for responsive email layouts.

### Typical emails
Welcome, email verification, password reset, order receipt, notifications. Each should have one clear call to action link.

### Rate limits
Providers cap sending speed; also protect your own endpoints (forgot-password) with rate limiting so attackers cannot use you to spam.
keyPoints: Create one transporter from env credentials
`sendMail` with `text` + `html`; verify the sender domain (SPF/DKIM)
Send in the background or via a queue with retries
Use jsonTransport/Mailpit/Ethereal for dev and tests
Rate-limit endpoints that trigger emails
pitfalls: Awaiting slow SMTP inside the request path for every user action
Sending from an unverified domain (spam folder)

examples.title: Email utility

interview.q: Why not send emails synchronously inside the request?
interview.a: SMTP calls are slow and can fail; users should not wait or see errors for them, so send in the background or enqueue a retryable job.
DNS-based mechanisms that prove your mail server is allowed to send for your domain (SPF) and that the message was not altered (DKIM), improving deliverability.

topics.title: Payments: Stripe Checkout and Webhooks
topics.summary: Create a Stripe Checkout session on the server and fulfil orders from a signature-verified webhook that uses the raw body.
topics.description:
Never process card details yourself. **Stripe Checkout** hosts the payment page; your server only creates a session and later learns the result.

### Flow
1. Client calls `POST /api/checkout` (authenticated).
2. Server loads the real prices **from your database** (never trust prices from the client), then calls `stripe.checkout.sessions.create({ mode: 'payment', line_items, success_url, cancel_url, metadata: { orderId } })`.
3. Server returns `session.url`; the browser redirects there.
4. After payment Stripe calls your **webhook** (`checkout.session.completed`).
5. The webhook handler marks the order paid and sends the receipt.

Do not rely on the success redirect to mark orders paid: users can close the tab. The webhook is the source of truth.

### Webhook rules
- Stripe signs each request. Verify with `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(rawBody, signatureHeader, endpointSecret)`.
- Signature verification needs the **raw body bytes**. So mount `express.raw({ type: 'application/json' })` on the webhook route **before** `express.json()` (or only apply `json()` to other routes). A parsed body will fail verification.
- Respond `2xx` quickly; do heavy work asynchronously. Stripe retries failures.
- Be **idempotent**: the same event can arrive more than once; store processed `event.id`s or make updates safe to repeat.
- Test locally with the Stripe CLI: `stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhooks/stripe`.

### Keys
Use the secret key (`sk_...`) only on the server and the publishable key on the front end; keep `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in env.
keyPoints: Create Checkout sessions server-side using prices from your DB
Webhook is the source of truth for payment success
Verify signatures with the RAW body: `express.raw()` before `express.json()`
Handlers must be idempotent and respond 2xx quickly
Test with `stripe listen`
pitfalls: Mounting `express.json()` globally before the webhook route (signature verification fails)
Trusting amounts or prices sent by the client
Fulfilling orders on the success page instead of the webhook

examples.title: Checkout and webhook

interview.q: Why must the webhook use express.raw?
interview.a: Stripe's signature is computed over the exact raw bytes; if express.json() parses the body first, re-serialising it changes the bytes and verification fails.

interview.q: Why use a webhook instead of the redirect to confirm payment?
interview.a: Users may close the browser or lose connection before the redirect, while the webhook is a reliable server-to-server notification that is retried until acknowledged.

topics.title: Scheduled Jobs and Background Tasks (cron)
topics.summary: Run recurring tasks with node-cron, and use queues or a separate worker for heavy or multi-instance workloads.
topics.description:
Some work does not start from an HTTP request: nightly cleanup, daily reports, expiring trials, reminder emails. **node-cron** schedules functions with a cron expression.

### Cron expression
Five fields: `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`.
| Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `* * * * *` | every minute |
| `*/15 * * * *` | every 15 minutes |
| `0 2 * * *` | daily at 02:00 |
| `0 9 * * 1` | Mondays at 09:00 |
| `0 0 1 * *` | first of every month |

Pass `{ timezone: 'Asia/Kolkata' }`, otherwise the server's time zone is used.

### Rules for jobs
- Wrap the body in `try/catch` and log: an unhandled rejection in a job can crash the process.
- Make jobs **idempotent** (running twice is harmless) and prevent overlap with a lock flag if a run can take longer than the interval.
- Do not schedule jobs in a serverless function: there is no always-on process. Use the platform scheduler (Vercel Cron, GitHub Actions, Render cron job) to hit a protected endpoint or run a script.

### Multiple instances
If you run 3 server instances, a cron inside the app runs **three times**. Options: run jobs in a dedicated worker process, use a distributed lock (Redis `SET NX`), or use a queue such as **BullMQ** (Redis) with repeatable jobs, retries and concurrency control.

### Queues for heavy work
Image processing, PDF generation and bulk email should be pushed to a queue and processed by workers, so the HTTP request returns immediately.
keyPoints: `cron.schedule('0 2 * * *', fn, { timezone })`
try/catch inside jobs; make them idempotent; avoid overlap
App-level cron runs once per instance: use a worker, lock or queue
Serverless needs platform schedulers instead of in-process cron
BullMQ gives retries, delays and repeatable jobs
pitfalls: Duplicate runs when the app is scaled to several instances
Forgetting the time zone, so jobs fire at unexpected hours
Long jobs overlapping with the next trigger

examples.title: node-cron jobs

interview.q: What problem appears when you run cron jobs inside a scaled Express app?
interview.a: Each instance runs the schedule, so the job executes multiple times; use a single worker, a distributed lock or a queue-based scheduler.
Jobs may run twice due to retries, restarts or overlap; idempotent logic ensures repeated runs do not corrupt data or duplicate effects.
